# Deep learning auto-segmentation of six thoracic organs at risk on multi-centre MRI with a MONAI SegResNet

*Draft — generated by `paper/dlas_6oar/build_manuscript.py`. Tables are read from `paper/dlas_6oar/tables/` (computed from the per-patient result files by `analysis_dlas.py`). Items in square brackets marked À COMPLÉTER must be completed by the authors.*

---

## Abstract

**Background and purpose.** MR-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) requires fast, reproducible contouring of organs at risk (OAR). We developed and evaluated a deep learning auto-segmentation (DLAS) model for six thoracic OAR on heterogeneous MRI.

**Materials and methods.** We used 115 diagnostic MRI examinations from four centres (TotalSegmentator MRI v2.0; 1.5 T and 3 T; gradient-echo and spin-echo sequences) with reference labels of both lungs, heart, oesophagus, spinal cord and aorta. A 3D SegResNet (MONAI, 18.8 million parameters) was trained with a Dice plus cross-entropy loss in 5-fold patient-level cross-validation. A capacity-matched 3D U-Net served as baseline. We computed the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) and average symmetric surface distance (ASSD) on the native grid, also within the lung slices for the spinal cord and aorta, and analysed failures.

**Results.** Median DSC was 0.944, 0.951, 0.896, 0.678, 0.881 and 0.897 for the left lung, right lung, heart, oesophagus, spinal cord and aorta. Median HD95 was 4.9, 4.3, 10.0, 7.9, 2.6 and 4.4 mm. Within the lung slices, spinal cord and aorta reached DSC 0.882 and 0.903. SegResNet exceeded the U-Net for every OAR. Thirty-one of 115 patients had at least one failure. Failures of the lungs, heart, spinal cord or aorta were more frequent with non-gradient-echo sequences (13/25 vs 10/90 patients, p < 0.001); oesophageal failures occurred in smaller reference volumes (median 4.8 vs 14.3 mL).

**Conclusions.** A single SegResNet segmented five of six thoracic OAR with DSC close to 0.9 on multi-centre, multi-sequence MRI. The oesophagus and atypical sequences remain the main limitations. Evaluation on MR-Linac images with clinical contours and physician grading is required before clinical use.

*Keywords:* MR-guided radiotherapy; auto-segmentation; organs at risk; deep learning; thorax.

---

## 1. Introduction

MR-guided radiotherapy combines a linear accelerator with an MRI scanner [1, 2]. It offers soft-tissue contrast, imaging in treatment position and daily online plan adaptation [3, 4]. In the thorax, MRI improves the visualisation of the tumour and of the heart and great vessels, and allows cardiac substructure sparing [5, 6]. Online adaptation on a 1.5 T MR-Linac is now used for lung cancer, but each adapted fraction requires the OAR to be checked or re-contoured while the patient lies on the couch [7].

Manual contouring is slow and variable. In thoracic oncology, training changes contour overlap substantially [8], and OAR contour variations change automatically generated treatment plans [9]. Inter-observer variability is highest for the oesophagus and spinal cord in Dice terms [10].

Deep learning auto-segmentation (DLAS) has been evaluated extensively on thoracic CT, including against atlas-based contouring [11] and in an international challenge [10], and whole-body CT models now cover most radiotherapy OAR [12, 13]. Models from several vendors trained on the same thoracic CT dataset have also been compared [14]. Reviews describe a shift from atlas-based to deep learning methods and the need for clinical evaluation beyond geometry [15, 16]. Self-configuring frameworks such as nnU-Net set strong baselines [17], and open frameworks such as MONAI provide reference architectures such as SegResNet [18, 19].

Thoracic DLAS on MRI is less studied. At 0.35 T, 3D U-Nets trained on planning MRI segmented six thoracic OAR with median DSC from 0.78 (oesophagus) to 0.96 (lungs) [20], and were implemented clinically with time savings [21]. Patient-specific fine-tuning further improved accuracy and accumulated dose [22], as in other MRgRT sites [23–25]. Cardiac MRI segmentation for MRgRT has also been reported [26, 27]. These thoracic models were trained on images from a single MR-Linac type. In the studies we reviewed, we did not find an evaluation of thoracic OAR segmentation across field strengths, vendors and sequences. The public TotalSegmentator MRI dataset contains such heterogeneous examinations [28].

**Objective.** We trained and evaluated a MONAI SegResNet for six thoracic OAR (left and right lungs, heart, oesophagus, spinal cord, aorta) on multi-centre, multi-sequence MRI. We report geometric accuracy, accuracy within the thoracic region, a capacity-matched U-Net baseline and a systematic analysis of failures.

## 2. Materials and methods

### 2.1 Database
- **Source.** TotalSegmentator MRI v2.0 (public; 616 MRI examinations; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.14710732) [28]. Reference labels are those released with the dataset; they are not clinical radiotherapy contours.
- **Four-OAR cohort.** Examinations with all four OAR (left lung, right lung, heart, oesophagus; ≥ 10 voxels each) and both lungs labelled: 187 patients.
- **Six-OAR cohort (this study).** Spinal cord and aorta were added from the same dataset on background voxels only, leaving the four original labels unchanged. Patients were kept when the spinal cord covered ≥ 95 % of the axial slices spanning the lungs and the aorta ≥ 95 % of the caudal 75 % of those slices. This left **115 patients**. These criteria select patients but do not crop the labels; the spinal cord and aorta often extend into the abdomen.
- **Imaging.** Diagnostic MRI from four centres, not MR-Linac images (Table 1). Native in-plane voxel size had a median of 1.19 mm.
- **Ethics.** Public, anonymised dataset. [À COMPLÉTER : statut éthique / dispense selon l'institution.]

### 2.2 Pre-processing
Images and labels were reoriented to RAS and resampled to 1.5 × 1.5 × 3 mm (bilinear for images, nearest neighbour for labels). Intensities were clipped to the 0.5th–99.5th percentiles and rescaled to [0, 1]. No bias-field correction or registration was applied.

### 2.3 Network implementation
- **Architecture.** MONAI SegResNet [18, 19]: 32 initial filters, encoder blocks [1, 2, 2, 4], decoder blocks [1, 1, 1], GroupNorm (8 groups), dropout 0.2, 7 output channels (background + 6 OAR); 18,796,167 parameters.
- **Baseline.** MONAI 3D U-Net with channels 48–96–192–384–832, strides 2, no residual units, InstanceNorm, PReLU; 18,808,159 parameters (capacity matched).
- **Loss.** Sum of a soft Dice loss and a cross-entropy loss with equal weights, computed on softmax probabilities, the Dice term excluding the background:

  L = L_Dice + L_CE,
  L_Dice = 1 − (1/C) Σ_c [ 2 Σ_i p_ic g_ic + ε ] / [ Σ_i p_ic + Σ_i g_ic + ε ],
  L_CE = − (1/N) Σ_i Σ_c g_ic log p_ic,

  where p_ic is the predicted probability of class c at voxel i, g_ic the one-hot reference, C = 6 foreground classes in the Dice term, N the number of voxels and ε a small smoothing constant (MONAI DiceCELoss defaults).
- **Environment.** MONAI 1.5.2, PyTorch 2.10.0 (CUDA 12.8), NVIDIA Tesla T4 (16 GB), Kaggle cloud notebooks.

### 2.4 Training strategy
- **Cross-validation.** Patient-level 5-fold cross-validation (KFold, shuffled, seed 42) on the sorted patient list; 23 validation patients per fold. Each patient was predicted once, by the model that did not see it during training. No separate test set was held out.
- **Sampling and augmentation.** Random 128 × 128 × 64 patches (positive:negative 2:1, two patches per volume), batch size 2. Augmentations: random affine (rotation ±0.26 rad, scaling ±10 %, p = 0.3), random 90° in-plane rotation (p = 0.2), gamma contrast 0.7–1.5 (p = 0.3), bias field (p = 0.2) and Gaussian noise (σ = 0.02, p = 0.2). Flipping was not used, to preserve left/right labels.
- **Optimisation.** AdamW (learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 1e-5), cosine annealing to 1e-6 over 150 epochs, mixed precision, gradient clipping at 1.0, training seed 42. The checkpoint with the best mean validation DSC was kept.
- **Hyperparameters.** All hyperparameters were fixed a priori and identical for both networks; no search was performed (Table 3).

**Table 3.** Hyperparameters.

| Parameter | Range tested | Final value |
|---|---|---|
| Voxel spacing | not tuned | 1.5 × 1.5 × 3 mm |
| Patch size | not tuned | 128 × 128 × 64 |
| Batch size | not tuned | 2 (2 patches per volume) |
| Optimiser | not tuned | AdamW |
| Learning rate (initial → final) | not tuned | 1e-4 → 1e-6 (cosine) |
| Weight decay | not tuned | 1e-5 |
| Epochs | not tuned | 150 |
| Loss | not tuned | Dice + cross-entropy (1:1) |
| Dropout (SegResNet) | not tuned | 0.2 |
| Normalisation (SegResNet) | not tuned | GroupNorm, 8 groups |
| Sliding-window overlap at inference | not tuned | 0.5, Gaussian weighting |

### 2.5 Post-processing
Inference used a sliding window (128 × 128 × 64, overlap 0.5, Gaussian weighting). The label map was the voxel-wise argmax, resampled to the native label grid with nearest-neighbour interpolation. No connected-component filtering or other post-processing was applied.

### 2.6 Evaluation
- **Geometric metrics** per patient and OAR on the native grid: DSC; HD95, defined as the maximum of the two directed 95th percentiles of boundary distances (mm); ASSD (mm), used here as the average Hausdorff distance; surface DSC at 2 mm [29]; relative volume error. Boundary points were extracted with a 6-connected erosion and distances computed between voxel centres.
- **Thoracic region.** Because the spinal-cord and aortic labels extend beyond the thorax, these two OAR were also evaluated within the slices containing lung in the reference. Overlap metrics used the voxels of these slices; surface metrics used boundary points in these slices, measured against the full boundary of the other mask.
- **Failure analysis.** Failure thresholds were set before the analysis: DSC < 0.7 for the lungs, heart, spinal cord and aorta, and DSC < 0.5 for the oesophagus, whose median DSC is close to 0.7 in published MRI series [20]. For each failure we recorded empty predictions, the fraction of the predicted volume outside its largest 26-connected component, the relative volume error and acquisition descriptors (sequence, study type, slice spacing).
- **Clinical grading.** [À COMPLÉTER : aucun grading clinique n'a été réalisé. Si un grading est ajouté : échelle (par ex. aucune correction / correction mineure / majeure), évaluateur(s), nombre de cas.]

### 2.7 Statistics
Results are reported as median [interquartile range]. SegResNet and U-Net were compared on the same patients (paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Holm correction over the six OAR). Associations between failures and acquisition factors were tested with Fisher's exact test (categorical) and the Mann–Whitney U test (continuous). Analyses used Python 3.11 (NumPy, pandas, SciPy).

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Training
- **SegResNet.** The best checkpoint occurred at epoch 144 (median; range 131–149) with a median best validation DSC of 0.838 over the six OAR. Training took 97 s per epoch (median), about 4.0 h per fold, on one T4 GPU.
- **U-Net.** Best epoch 133 (116–145), best validation DSC 0.722, 47 s per epoch, about 2.0 h per fold.
- **Inference.** Median 4.4 s per patient for SegResNet and 0.9 s for the U-Net (sliding window on the T4, excluding data loading).
- Learning curves are shown in Fig. 3.

### 3.4 Failures
- **Frequency.** 31 of 115 patients (27 %) had at least one failure: left lung 9, right lung 10, heart 11, oesophagus 16, spinal cord 5 and aorta 8 patients. Eight patients failed for both the oesophagus and another OAR. One prediction was empty (oesophagus).
- **Sequence.** Failures of the lungs, heart, spinal cord or aorta occurred in 13 of 25 patients imaged with a non-gradient-echo sequence (spin echo, "RM" or unknown) versus 10 of 90 with gradient echo (Fisher p < 0.001). All three spine examinations failed for at least one of these OAR.
- **Oesophagus.** Failed cases had smaller reference volumes (median 4.8 vs 14.3 mL, Mann–Whitney p < 0.001). One failed case had a reference oesophageal volume of 100.9 mL, about eight times the cohort median, which suggests a reference annotation error.
- **Error types (Table 6).** Most failures combined fragmentation (a large share of the predicted volume outside the largest component) with under- or over-segmentation. The worst case (PATIENT_s0108, spine examination, spin echo) had heart DSC 0.000 and lung DSC 0.35–0.36 (Fig. 4).

## 4. Discussion

### 4.1 Comparison with the literature
**Table 7.** Comparison with published thoracic OAR auto-segmentation (median or mean DSC as reported; HD95 in mm). Studies differ in modality, image type, reference contours and test design, so values are not directly comparable.

| Study | Modality and setting | n (test) | Left lung | Right lung | Heart | Oesophagus | Spinal cord | Aorta |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| This study (SegResNet) | Diagnostic MRI, 4 centres, 1.5/3 T; 5-fold CV | 115 | 0.944 (4.9) | 0.951 (4.3) | 0.896 (10.0) | 0.678 (7.9) | 0.881 (2.6); thorax 0.882 (2.5) | 0.897 (4.4); thorax 0.903 (3.2) |
| Ribeiro et al. 2023 [20] | 0.35 T MR-Linac planning MRI, single centre; 3D U-Nets | 23 | 0.96 (3.9) | 0.96 (5.3) | 0.94 (5.8) | 0.78 (3.5) | 0.88 (2.6) (a) | 0.90 (3.0) |
| Yang et al. 2018, AAPM challenge [10] | Planning CT; best methods | [À COMPLÉTER] | 0.95–0.98 (b) | 0.95–0.98 (b) | [À COMPLÉTER] | 0.55–0.72 (b) | [À COMPLÉTER] | — |
| Francis et al. 2022 [30] | Thoracic CT; two-stage 3D U-Net | [À COMPLÉTER] | — | — | 0.941 | — | — | — |
| Summerfield et al. 2024 [27] | 0.35 T MR-Linac; cardiac substructures | [À COMPLÉTER] | — | — | chambers 0.85 (mean) | — | — | — |
| Akinci D'Antonoli et al. 2025 [28] | Multi-sequence MRI; nnU-Net, 80 structures | internal test | mean DSC 0.839 over 80 structures (per-OAR values not extracted) | | | | | |

(a) Spinal canal. (b) Range of the averages of the participating methods. Values were taken from the abstracts retrieved from PubMed; [À COMPLÉTER] marks values not available in the abstract.

- **Lungs, heart and aorta.** Our median DSC values are 0.003–0.044 below those obtained on 0.35 T planning MRI (largest difference for the heart) [20]. Our images were heterogeneous diagnostic examinations, and our reference labels were not clinical contours.
- **Spinal cord.** DSC (0.88) and HD95 (2.6 mm) match those reported for the spinal canal at 0.35 T [20]. The structures differ (cord vs canal).
- **Oesophagus.** Our median DSC (0.68) is lower than at 0.35 T (0.78) [20] and within the range of CT challenge methods (0.55–0.72) [10]. The oesophagus is the OAR with the highest inter-observer variability [10], and our failures were concentrated in small reference volumes.
- **Baseline.** The capacity-matched U-Net was worse for every OAR, mostly through distant false positives (median lung HD95 15.5 vs 4.9 mm). SegResNet also outperformed U-Net variants for pelvic CT OAR in MONAI [31] and has been used on Unity cine MRI [32].

### 4.2 Interpretation per OAR
- **Lungs.** High DSC with occasional large HD95 driven by fragments or by atypical acquisitions; the field of view sometimes contained only part of the lungs (abdominal examinations).
- **Heart.** DSC 0.896 but the largest HD95 (10.0 mm). The heart's boundary with the great vessels and the diaphragm is ill-defined on diagnostic MRI, and two heart failures had volumes reduced by more than 90 % on spine examinations.
- **Oesophagus.** The smallest and lowest-contrast structure. Volume error was positive (+7.9 %), suggesting over-inclusion of surrounding tissue.
- **Spinal cord and aorta.** Accurate within and outside the thorax; the thoracic-region values were slightly higher, so the global result is not driven by the abdominal segments.

### 4.3 Failure analysis
Failures clustered in non-gradient-echo sequences and spine examinations. The training set was dominated by gradient-echo images (90 of 115 patients), so these sequences were under-represented. Our failure causes were derived from the result files and remain probable, not confirmed by visual review of every case. Fragmentation was frequent; a largest-component filter could remove some false positives, but we did not apply post-processing in order to report the raw network output.

### 4.4 Limitations
1. **Reference standard.** Labels from a public dataset, not clinical radiotherapy contours; one suspected annotation error was found.
2. **Images.** Diagnostic MRI, not MR-Linac (0.35 T or 1.5 T Unity) images; no planning or daily adaptive scans.
3. **Validation.** Cross-validation only; the best checkpoint was selected on the validation fold that was also used for reporting, which may bias results upwards. No external test set.
4. **Cohort size and selection.** 115 patients selected on annotation completeness; age and sex were missing for 33 patients each (29 %).
5. **No clinical grading or dosimetric evaluation.** Geometric metrics correlate imperfectly with clinical usefulness and editing time [33–35]; metric choice must follow the clinical question [36, 37].
6. **Single training seed and fixed hyperparameters.** No tuning; an nnU-Net comparison was not performed in this cohort [17].

### 4.5 Perspectives
- **Time savings.** DLAS reduced contouring time at the 0.35 T MR-Linac [21] and in MR-guided prostate radiotherapy [38]. Measuring editing time on our model's contours requires clinical users.
- **Patient-specific fine-tuning.** Fine-tuning on the planning MRI improved daily segmentation and accumulated dose at 0.35 T [22–24]. A multi-centre base model such as ours could serve as the starting point. Deep learning contour propagation from the planning to the daily MRI is an alternative for fractionated lung MRgRT [39].
- **Dosimetry.** The impact of contour errors on dose [9] should be assessed, especially for the oesophagus and heart.
- **MR-Linac validation.** [À COMPLÉTER : jeu de données Unity 1,5 T avec contours cliniques, si disponible.]

---

## 5. Conclusion
A MONAI SegResNet trained on 115 multi-centre, multi-sequence MRI examinations segmented the lungs, heart, spinal cord and aorta with median DSC 0.88–0.95 and the oesophagus with 0.68. It outperformed a capacity-matched U-Net for every OAR. Failures concentrated in non-gradient-echo sequences and small oesophageal volumes. Validation on MR-Linac images with clinical contours, physician grading and dosimetric evaluation is the next step.
